# Page 2^page=2
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Why software engineering is important • Software is everywhere and our society is now totally dependent on software-intensive systems • Society could not function without software • Healthcare Systems • Transportation Systems • Energy Systems • Manufacturing Systems • … • Software failures cannot be tolerated… but they still happen! SE - Introduction 2

# Page 3^page=3
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Example: worldwide IT outage on July 19, 2024 • CrowdStrike crashed enterprise Windows-based systems worldwide (approximately 8.5 million devices) • Airlines including American Airlines, Delta, KLM, Lufthansa, Ryanair, SAS, and United • Airports (e.g., Gatwick, Luton), healthcare, and media organizations (e.g., MTV, Sky, BBC) • Financial organizations including the London Stock Exchange, Lloyds Bank, and Visa • Sporting bodies including F1 teams (e.g., Aston Martin, Mercedes, and Williams) and the Paris 2024 Olympic Organizing Committee • Array out of bounds read issue! • https://www.computerweekly.com/feature/CrowdStrike-update- chaos-explained-What-you-need-to-know • https://www.crowdstrike.com/wp- content/uploads/2024/08/Channel-File-291-Incident-Root-Cause- Analysis-08.06.2024.pdf SE - Introduction 3

# Page 4^page=4
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Software engineering: definition • Field of computer science dealing with software systems • large and complex • built by teams • exist in many versions • last many years • undergo changes • Multi-person construction of multi-version software SE - Introduction 8

# Page 5^page=5
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Software engineer: required skills • Programming skills not enough! • Programmer: • develops a complete program • works on known specifications • works individually • Software engineer: • identifies requirements and develops specifications • designs a component to be combined with other components, developed, maintained, used by others; component can become part of several systems • collaborates with others to ensure components show adequate qualities • works in a team SE - Introduction 9

# Page 6^page=6
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Skills of software engineers • Technical • Project management • Cognitive • Enterprise organization • Interaction with different cultures • Domain knowledge • The quality of human resources is of primary importance SE - Introduction 10

# Page 7^page=7
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi The software product • Different from traditional types of products • intangible • difficult to describe and evaluate • malleable • human intensive • does not involve any trivial manufacturing process • Aspects affecting product quality SE - Introduction 12 Product quality Development technology Process quality People quality Cost, time, and schedule

M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Process qualities: timeliness • Ability to respond to change requests in a timely fashion SE - Introduction 15

# Page 11^page=11
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Software lifecycles • Initially, no reference model: Just code & fix • As a reaction to the many problems: traditional “waterfall” model • identify phases and activities • force linear progression from a phase to the next • no returns (they are harmful) • better planning and control • standardize outputs (artifacts) from each phase • Software like manufacturing • Then, flexible processes: iterative models, agile methods, DevOps SE - Introduction 16

# Page 12^page=12
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi A waterfall organization SE - Introduction Feasibility Study Requirements Analysis & Specification Design Coding & Unit Test Integration & System Test Deployment Maintenance 17 High phases Low phases

# Page 13^page=13
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Effort distribution (van Vliet 2008) SE - Introduction V&V 45% coding 20%design 15% requirements engineering 10% specification 10% 23

# Page 14^page=14
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Maintenance • Corrective maintenance: deals with the repair of faults or defects found ≈ 20% • Evolution • adaptive maintenance: consists of adapting software to changes in the environment (the hardware or the operating system, business rules, government policies…) ≈ 20% • perfective maintenance: mainly deals with accommodating to new or changed user requirements ≈ 50% • preventive maintenance: concerns activities aimed at increasing the system’s maintainability ≈ 10% SE - Introduction 24

# Page 15^page=15
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Correction vs evolution • Distinction can be unclear, because specifications are often incomplete and ambiguous • This causes problems because specs are often part of a contract between developer and customer • early frozen specs can be problematic, because they are more likely to be wrong SE - Introduction 25

# Page 16^page=16
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Problems of software evolution • It is (almost) never anticipated and planned; this causes disasters • Software is very easy to change • often, under emergency, changes are applied directly to code • inconsistent state of project documents SE - Introduction 26

# Page 17^page=17
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi How to face evolution • Good engineering practice: • first modify design, then change implementation • apply changes consistently in all documents • Likely changes must be anticipated • Software must be designed to accommodate changes in a cost- effective way • This is one of the main goals of software engineering SE - Introduction 27
